import { Aside, CardGrid, LinkCard } from '@astrojs/starlight/components';

**Task:** announce that something changed so clients (and optionally other
methods of your app) can react.

## Declare an event

An event type is an enum marked `#[app::event]`. Wire it into your state with the
`emits` argument so the macro knows which events the app produces:

```rust
#[app::state(emits = for<'a> Event<'a>)]
pub struct KvStore {
    items: UnorderedMap<String, LwwRegister<String>>,
    handler_counter: Counter,
}

#[app::event]
pub enum Event<'a> {
    Inserted { key: &'a str, value: &'a str },
    Updated { key: &'a str, value: &'a str },
    Removed { key: &'a str },
    Cleared,
}
```

## Emit it

Call `app::emit!` with a variant. The event is part of the call's outcome: the call's answer carries it, and clients following the app's event stream receive it once the entry commits:

```rust
app::emit!(Event::Updated { key: &key, value: &value });
```

## Run a handler when it fires

To also invoke one of your own methods when the event is emitted, use the tuple
form `(event, "handler_name")`. The handler is a method named by that string and
marked `#[app::handler]`; its parameters match the event variant's fields. After
the entry commits, the app's leader runs it **once**, as a call of the app
itself (caller `App`, not the member who emitted), with the event's data as its
arguments ([Event handlers](/protocol/xcall/)). This pattern is
`apps/kv-store-with-handlers`:

```rust
#[app::logic]
impl KvStore {
    pub fn set(&mut self, key: String, value: String) -> app::Result<()> {
        if self.items.contains(&key)? {
            app::emit!((
                Event::Updated { key: &key, value: &value },
                "update_handler"
            ));
        } else {
            app::emit!((
                Event::Inserted { key: &key, value: &value },
                "insert_handler"
            ));
        }
        self.items.insert(key, value.into())?;
        Ok(())
    }

    // handler: name matches the string above; params match the variant fields
    #[app::handler]
    pub fn update_handler(&mut self, key: &str, value: &str) -> app::Result<()> {
        app::log!("Handler 'update_handler' called: key={key}, value={value}");
        self.handler_counter.increment()?;
        Ok(())
    }

    #[app::handler]
    pub fn insert_handler(&mut self, key: &str, value: &str) -> app::Result<()> {
        app::log!("Handler 'insert_handler' called: key={key}, value={value}");
        self.handler_counter.increment()?;
        Ok(())
    }
}
```

<Aside type="caution" title="Only declared handlers run">
  The node runs a handler only if the app's ABI declares that method
  `#[app::handler]`. An event naming any other method, or an app built without
  an embedded ABI, runs nothing. So mark every method an `emit!` names (an
  unmarked method of the same impl, or a private one, is a compile error).
</Aside>

<Aside type="note" title="Handlers change only this app's state">
  A handler is just another method, so it can write state: here it bumps a
  `Counter`. It runs as the app, so `env::account_id()` there is the app's own
  id, not the emitter's: pass what it needs in the event's fields. A handler
  that fails is recorded with its error and not retried. Use the plain
  one-argument `emit!` when you only want to notify clients, and the tuple form
  when you also want in-app logic to run.
</Aside>

<Aside type="caution" title="An event says what the method put in it">
  An event's fields are whatever the emitting method wrote into them. If the
  method copies a field such as `sender` or `author` from its arguments, the
  caller chose it. Fill identity fields from `env::account_id()` in the method,
  or read who did something from authored state, such as the owner an
  [`Authored`](/build/choosing-state/) collection records for each entry.
</Aside>

## Exercise it

```sh
meroctl call -c my-kv set --args '{"key": "hello", "value": "world"}'
meroctl context watch my-kv
```

The call's answer lists the events it emitted, and `context watch` prints the
app's committed events from the start of its event ring, then live ones, as
JSON lines. A handler the event names runs after the entry commits, as its own
entry.

## Worked example: a chat notification flow

A messaging app emits `MessageSent` whenever a member posts, and a web client
follows the app's event stream to render new messages the moment they land. The
event and the method that emits it:

```rust
#[app::event]
pub enum Event<'a> {
    MessageSent { from: &'a str, text: &'a str },
}

#[app::logic]
impl Chat {
    pub fn send_message(&mut self, text: String) -> app::Result<()> {
        let from = hex::encode(env::account_id());    // the caller, never an argument
        self.messages.push(text.clone())?;
        app::emit!(Event::MessageSent { from: &from, text: &text });
        Ok(())
    }
}
```

A client follows the stream with mero-js. `events(app, from)` is the node's
`GET /apps/{app}/events?from=N`, a server-sent event stream sealed like every
other answer: first the events the app's ring still holds from entry `from` on,
then live ones as entries commit ([Reads](/protocol/reads/#events)):

```js
for await (const ev of client.events(appId, 0)) {   // { id: "index:seq", kind, data }
  if (ev.kind === 'MessageSent') {
    const { from, text } = ev.data;                  // the variant's fields, as JSON
    renderMessage(from, text);
  }
}
```

Each event has:

- `id`, `index:seq`: the entry that emitted it and its position in that entry.
  A client that reconnects passes the last index it saw as `from` and misses
  nothing the ring still holds.
- `kind`, the variant name: here `"MessageSent"`.
- `data`, the variant's fields.

Everyone who reaches the app receives all of its events, so do not put in an
event what some members may not see.
